assessments.reasoning: The PolyForm Project license-library file at commit a2316cfa35d3947fdc5af4bcc1f321662bfd79d8 is primary historical evidence for the 1.0.0 side. Its title, /perimeter/1.0.0 link and plural wording agree. Capture d5b4284305934fd3a83d3c661fb9f2b0 covers 4,531 bytes, SHA-256 8ead8ddb75d93c22b1281901ae09fad975c8c2302480393480d116f8cbb990b1.

The publisher’s pinned site file licenses/perimeter/1.0.1.txt supplies the second observation. Its 1.0.1 heading and link accompany the singular wording. Capture 1593ccfe4b9b4227ac79b999a06117b0 covers 4,529 bytes.

challenge.method: Compared each file’s heading, embedded edition URL and full porting sentence, testing whether a filename change alone could explain the apparent edition difference.
challenge.results: Both bodies independently identify their respective edition, and both nouns in the porting example change from plural to singular. The wording difference survives comparison without relying on filenames.

limitations: The comparison establishes wording in the two captured representations. Publication dates, authorship, legal equivalence and the significance of the change remain outside its scope.

For all nine assessments, I inspected the complete Software Commons Evidence Standard (policy_standard), Codex Research Protocol (policy_protocol) and SCES-1.0 research task brief (policy_task_brief), in that order, at commit ab26f278422772f2d9e5d4dd016407d14372a710. The adopted bundle SHA-256 was supplied as 14da3f31f697ab828d4a4560f060dbe511861020db54bea7bc531e20ea0855ce. The five publisher bodies supplied the domain evidence. Enforceability, individual product status, text reuse and canonical admission were outside the review.
reasoning: The two pinned publisher files identify different Perimeter editions in both the heading and the link immediately below it. In the Competition porting example, 1.0.0 reads “a different platforms or programming languages” and 1.0.1 reads “a different platform or programming language.”
